summary:
Amazonas stands under Peru's national framework: the department has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern, and none of the sources covering this territory contain Amazonas-specific content. What a trans visitor faces in Amazonas is the national statute book, national policing and national monitoring data.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities. On 20 February 2025 the Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The text still required plenary backing at that point, and the reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho argued the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes, whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The April 2025 law mandates that restroom entry be determined by biological sex, barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors.

The restriction reaches private life as well as public facilities. IDEHPUCP recalls SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, in which a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. IDEHPUCP also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. IDEHPUCP finds the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity and implicitly framing them as harassment risks.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian, with 19 killings in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women. Killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The February 2023 murder of trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano (31), kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, followed the shooting of Priscila Aguado Huatuco (30) days earlier; two killers were arrested in March 2023. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

localsOnly:
Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, which shapes what documents a resident can hold and what the DNI shows when restroom access is policed by identity document.

Discrimination complaints can be lodged with the national consumer-protection body, but the route has produced a dismissal: SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 rejected a trans woman's complaint against SmartFit over bathroom assignment based on DNI sex markers.

In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, a change directed at trans patients in healthcare settings.

In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional after an activist legal challenge, establishing that judicial review of equality claims remains available.

The state does not record sexual orientation or gender identity in its crime-registration systems, so residents reporting an attack cannot have the motive registered or prosecuted as a hate crime.

Article 4 of the April 2025 law bans media and advertising content under vague child-protection terms, and the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years, exposure that falls on residents producing identity-related artistic, educational or advocacy material.
outOfScopeNotes:
None of the sources covering Amazonas contain department-level content; there is no sourced account of how the national restroom restriction is enforced in Amazonas, and local police or municipal practice there is unresolved rather than confirmed absent.

The inventory does not state whether the April 2025 restroom provision has been challenged in court beyond the July 2025 ruling against a separate anti-equality decree, or whether that ruling affects Article 5.1; this is unresolved.

Whether the 2017 hate-crime repeal has been revisited since, and whether any bill to restore LGBT coverage has reached a vote, is not sourced here.

Enforcement figures for the restroom rule, including any prosecutions or ejections, are not in the inventory; the DNI-check scenario is an activist's stated concern rather than a documented enforcement record.

The claim that recorded hate-crime figures are a sub-registry rests on one co-author's public statement; no alternative count is available in the sources.
